title: Cautious optimism for deep parameterized quantum circuits
authors: Marie Kempkes, Elies Gil-Fuster, Carlos Bravo-Prieto, Aroosa Ijaz, Alissa Wilms, Jens Eisert, Evert van Nieuwenburg, Vedran Dunjko
abstract: A central challenge in quantum machine learning is understanding the scaling behavior of parameterized quantum circuits (PQCs). In particular, it remains unclear how their performance on unseen data changes as the number of trainable parameters increases. Prior works have derived formal generalization guarantees for quantum models, but it is well-known that many such results do not fully characterize generalization behavior in practice. In this work, we show that gradient-based PQCs can exhibit improved performance on unseen data as model size increases, displaying the phenomenon of double descent. This contrasts with the traditional view that larger models lead to degraded generalization. We provide analytical results rigorously underpinning this behavior by leveraging add-one-in perturbation techniques and spectral properties of random matrices. We support these results with numerical experiments on re-uploading PQCs across several data sets and training set sizes, consistently observing the predicted double descent behavior. While other obstacles on the path toward practical quantum machine learning remain, our finding that deeper parameterized quantum circuits do not necessarily exhibit degraded performance provides reasons for cautious optimism.
summary: This paper investigates the generalization capabilities of parameterized quantum circuits by analyzing their scaling behavior with model size. Using advanced random matrix theory and spectral analysis, the authors prove that these circuits can exhibit a double descent phenomenon. This suggests that increasing circuit depth/parameters does not automatically lead to performance degradation in practice.
main_problem: The central challenge is understanding how the generalization performance of parameterized quantum circuits (PQCs) scales with an increasing number of trainable parameters.
main_result: The authors show that gradient-based PQCs can exhibit a double descent phenomenon, meaning their test error does not necessarily degrade as model size increases past the interpolation threshold.
method: The analysis combines rigorous theoretical derivations using add-one-in perturbation techniques and spectral properties of random matrices to bound the expected risk. These bounds are then compared against numerical results.
model_or_system: The study focuses on data re-uploading PQCs, where the quantum state $ho(x; \vartheta)$ depends on input data $x$ and trainable parameters $\vartheta$. The performance is measured by minimizing an expected risk function.
key_observables: Expected risk ($L(\vartheta)$) vs. model size ($p$), test loss, and eigenvalues of sample covariance/Hessian matrices.
important_parameters: Number of trainable parameters ($p$), training set size ($N$), the ratio $p/N$, and the interpolation threshold ($p=NK$).
main_assumptions: The analysis relies on asymptotic limits ($N, p 	o \infty$) and several technical assumptions regarding spectral properties (e.g., Assumptions 1-7) and local minima existence.
figures_summary: Numerical experiments consistently observe the predicted double descent behavior across multiple datasets, showing test loss peaking near the interpolation threshold ($p=NK$).
paper_structure: The paper develops theoretical lower and upper bounds on the expected risk using spectral analysis. It then demonstrates that these derived bounds exhibit a maximum at $p=N$ (or $p=NK$), confirming double descent behavior both theoretically and numerically.
why_interesting: This work connects concepts from classical overparameterized neural networks (double descent) to quantum machine learning models, providing theoretical grounding for the utility of very large, complex quantum circuits.

figures.caption: Figure 1. Test loss as a function of the number of parameters p for (a) MNIST-1D and (b) Fashion MNIST classification, and (c) a multi- dimensional synthetic regression task, for different training set sizes N. Vertical dashed lines indicate the predicted interpolation thresholds p = NK. In all three tasks, the test loss peaks close to interpolation and decreases again in the overparameterized regime, displaying a characteristic double descent profile. The shaded areas correspond to the standard deviation for ten independent experiment repetitions, each using independently sampled training data.
